sections.heading: Thanking you that I know you now
sections.text: Glorious God, I thank you that I know you. For so long I lived in your world without recognizing you. I received your gifts every day and did not see your hand. I stood in the light and was still blind. I heard countless sounds, but not your voice. I learned many things, but I did not understand your ways. I saw the world you made, but I did not see Jesus as my life and hope.
theological_themes: God is the Creator and Provider, even when people fail to acknowledge him.
Spiritual ignorance is deeper than lack of information; it is blindness to God and to Christ.
Knowing God is a gift worthy of gratitude.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that God made the world, gives life and everything else, and is near to all people. This supports the prayer’s confession that I was living inside God’s generous providence without knowing the Provider.

Paul describes unbelief as blindness to the glory of Christ, and conversion as God giving light in the heart. This directly illuminates the prayer’s movement from seeing the world without seeing Christ to receiving spiritual sight.

sections.heading: Remembering how you called me by grace
sections.text: I bless you for the day when, in your sovereign love, you looked on me and called me by grace. What was dead in me began to live. My darkened eyes began to see. My dull ears began to catch the sound of your voice. I turned toward you and found that you were already ready to hear me, ready to save me, and full of mercy.
theological_themes: Salvation begins with God’s gracious initiative, not human worthiness.
Regeneration is God giving life where there was spiritual death.
God welcomes sinners who turn to him.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says God makes sinners alive with Christ while they are dead in trespasses, because of his mercy and love. This grounds the prayer’s picture of a dead heart beginning to beat by grace.
Jesus teaches that coming to him depends on the Father drawing a person. This supports the prayer’s emphasis that God’s loving call came before and underneath my turning to him.

sections.heading: Letting your holiness tell me the truth about my sin
sections.text: When your grace opened my eyes, I also saw what I really was. My heart had been against you. I had resisted and grieved your Spirit. I fell before you and heard the truth I could not escape: sin deserves death. And as terrifying as your justice was, I saw that it was right. You hate sin because you are holy, and your holiness taught my stubborn will to bow before you. My thoughts accused me, and I could not heal myself.
theological_themes: Grace exposes sin rather than hiding it.
God’s judgment against sin is just because God is holy.
True conviction humbles the will before God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the mind set on the flesh as hostile to God and unable to please him. This gives biblical shape to the prayer’s confession that my heart was not merely weak but opposed to God.
This passage states God’s just moral judgment that the soul who sins shall die. The prayer echoes that verdict as the moment when God’s holiness and justice became personally unavoidable.
Paul warns believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit, showing that sin is personally offensive to God’s Spirit. This supports the prayer’s language about having vexed or grieved him.

sections.heading: Finding everything in the death of your Son
sections.text: Then you came near to me with a gentleness I did not expect. You showed me your Son dying so that I might live. In his death I found what I could never provide for myself: pardon, peace, righteousness, and hope. The gospel reached the place in me that nothing else could reach, and by your mercy I lived.
theological_themes: Christ’s death is the sinner’s life and peace with God.
The gospel brings saving power where self-repair cannot.
God’s mercy comes through the atoning work of Jesus.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says Christ died for the ungodly and that sinners are reconciled to God through his death. This grounds the prayer’s wonder that the Son died so I might live and have peace with God.

Peter connects Christ bearing sins in his body with believers dying to sin and living to righteousness. This supports the prayer’s claim that Christ’s death is not an idea at a distance but the place where life is found.

sections.heading: Holding on to Christ and speaking of your mercy
sections.text: Father, keep that peace fresh in my memory. Let me never treat mercy as a small thing. Hold me fast in Christ, and teach me to cling to him with faith. As long as I live, make me glad to tell others what you have done: you pardon sinners, you take in the blasphemer and the ungodly, and you wash people clean from their deepest stains. Let my tears over sin become praise for mercy found.
theological_themes: Assurance rests in Christ holding his people, not in human strength alone.
Forgiven sinners are called to witness to God’s mercy.
God’s grace is able to pardon even deep and shameful sin.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus promises that his sheep are held securely in his and the Father’s hand. This supports the prayer’s confidence that Christ’s grip on me is stronger than my grip on him.

Paul presents himself as a former blasphemer who received mercy so that Christ’s patience would be displayed to others. This strongly supports the prayer’s desire to tell others that God pardons even blasphemers and the ungodly.
John teaches that the blood of Jesus cleanses from sin and that God forgives those who confess. This grounds the prayer’s language of being washed from the deepest stain.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly emphasizes God’s sovereign initiative in conversion. That is preserved, though Christians from different theological traditions may frame the mechanics of grace and human response differently.

The line about never losing my hold on Christ or Christ’s hold on me was rendered with emphasis on Christ holding the believer securely, while still asking for persevering faith. This preserves assurance without implying self-sustained perseverance.

The original’s severe language about divine justice and the sinner deserving death was retained in substance. It may feel stark to modern readers, but it is central to the prayer’s movement from conviction to mercy.
significant_interpretive_choices: The original image of being surrounded by providences but not knowing the Provider was rendered as receiving God’s daily gifts without seeing his hand, to keep the concrete sense of dependence on God in ordinary life.

The phrase about God coming in “silken robes of love” was interpreted as God approaching the convicted sinner with unexpected gentleness and mercy through Christ, rather than as a separate mystical experience.

The “gospel cornet” image was rendered as the gospel reaching the heart with a new sound, preserving the idea of a summons or announcement without retaining an archaic instrument image that would distract contemporary readers.
